They try to make sure you're comfortable when you visit, share their concerns about their children's education and well being, and do their best to make sure your visit is enjoyable. I am dismayed by the platitudes and fixed prejudices shown in both the article and certainly in the responses. Of course Burnham has no magic wand to transform decades of problems. (Nor, of course, does any potential leader of the USA). At present one of the major issues is the effect of Brexit - on every part of the economy and on public life.
But  looking at how this has been presented: as ever there is confusion and conflation of Britain / England. This is a fundamental problem. The United Kingdom, as it is officially known, comprises England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. However the main political parties at the Westminster Parliament, together with the press, constantly undermine the smaller nations whom they treat with a lot of disrespect. Recent election results have shown that the three smaller nations favour political parties which want independence, or in the case of Northern Ireland, re-unification with the rest of Ireland. That may well be the greatest problem facing Burnham, but he has ruled out even considering it. It is an existential question which needs calm and conciliatory debate on all sides. comments.name: Alan
comments.body: The Blairites did more damage to the lives of ordinary people and to institutions like local government and the NHS than Thatcher and her ilk. Private-public partnerships were more of a capitalist giveaway than experienced in post Soviet Russia, Poland and the Ukraine and had similar effects, viz. enriching and empowering corporations, many foreign, at the expense of the taxpayer and accountability to the citizenry. Inequality soared, asset prices shot up, plutocrats were born and ordinary people were immiserated -- standards of living frozen or falling and life expectancies declining. Meanwhile, huge swathes of less well off people in Britain have bunked off on the dole, claiming disability and inability to work. Much of this is psycho-social, a reaction to joblessness and the apparent bleakness of prospects, especially for the young, the majority of whom now report pessimism, depression, anxiety and sundry health problems. Racism and ethnic antagonisms are once again boiling away alongside anti-immigrant sentiment and widespread cynicism about politics and government. Social media add more and more fuel to fires of anger and despair. BREXIT crippled much of the UK economy and an unfriendly US offers no relief. Steel and car making are on the ropes; the end of manufacturing in Britain is in sight. Finance, the great engine, is corrupt and parasitic on the real economy but now virtually the only source of wealth. So "no", not much can or will change for the better.

Between the developed south and the far north are vast expanses of boreal forest and taiga that are largely uninhabited with the exception of small indigenous communities in scattered locations and the occasional mining site. 

Fires are a natural part of this northern ecosystem. They are regularly started by lightening strikes. In the past, before the excessive warming and drying of recent years, they’d burn at low intensity and would burn out on their own. Today, northern Canada is highly affected by climate change and these huge remote forests are now dry and warm so the fires can grow uncontrollably. There’s no easy way to access these fires and put them out. The defect plays the role of curvature, which in Einstein's theory is MASS. Hexagons are flat, they have mass 0, they make a  bathroom floor tiling. The rotating ball in the article has 12 black pentagons, so the total defect, or mass, is 12 x 1 =12. Same in a dodecahedron. A cube has 6 faces which are squares, each of defect 6-4=2, so again the total defect is 6 x 2 =12. A tetrahedron has 4 faces each of defect 6-3=3, for a total of 4 x 3 =12.

Some models of space-time-matter require averaging all possible masses. To make sense of that, we use patches on soccer balls...

One way to understand how much of our weather is changed by global warming was discussed in 2012 in a TED Talk by NASA's former lead climate scientist James Hansen.

“Global warming is already affecting people. The Texas, Oklahoma, Mexico heatwave and drought last year, Moscow the year before and Europe in 2003, were all exceptional events, more than three standard deviations outside the norm. 

Fifty years ago, such anomalies covered only two- to three-tenths of one percent of the land area. In recent years, because of global warming, they now cover about 10 percent -- an increase by a factor of 25 to 50. So we can say with a high degree of confidence that the severe Texas and Moscow heatwaves were not natural; they were caused by global warming.”

That was in 2012 when these anomalies covered 10 percent of the land area. Nowadays they cover more than 20 percent of the land area.

Against that backdrop, criticism from Trump over a dubious issue is unlikely to be viewed as a major concern. If anything, Beijing may see little reason to respond while Washington remains preoccupied with its own mistakes.

As an aging  boomer and lifelong baseball addict I have to admit that I never, ever thought soccer would attain this level of popularity in the U.S. I still have no interest in the sport but I fully realize I'm in a small and ever shrinking cohort of American sports fans that will age out of the population in the next few decades. 

There was no youth soccer in my town and the high school didn't have a team. I'd been playing organized baseball, backyard football and pickup basketball seemingly forever by the time I ever saw or kicked a real soccer ball at about age 14.  I'd only glimpsed soccer a few times on the old ABC Wide World of Sports where it seemed a "foreign game" not so much in terms of geographic distance but in its seemingly bizarre rules: (You can't use your hands? Are you serious? What's up with that?) Back then soccer seemed to me more akin to a team version of blindfolded pin-the-tail-on-the-donkey or a three-legged race than a "real" eye-hand sport like baseball, (American) football, basketball or hockey, all of which I followed closely. 

The sports magazines I regularly consumed in the 60s and early 70s sometimes featured articles speculating on why soccer had so little appeal in America while the rest of the world couldn't get enough of it. There was no mystery in that to me. 

Times change, personal horizons broaden, and old biases fall away.  I don't think I'll ever become a soccer fan, but I now understand why others do.

EMS receives over 6,000 calls a day and don’t have the workforce to match. Out of 661 ambulances, only about 300 are active on a good day. 10-15 members leave per WEEK.

If paid the same scale as their fire side colleagues, they wouldn’t have to leave in search of better pay. 

Over 90% of calls are medical emergencies requiring EMS, so why aren’t they being paid like it?

EMTs and paramedics are trained and licensed medical professionals and they’re being paid less than UberEats drivers. Canada has about 9% of the world's forests, much of it remote and inaccessible.  You can't "manage" a vast forest wilderness as these uninformed politicians seem to think.  We could airdrop crews into remote areas for decades and come nowhere close to preventing wildfires, the overwhelming majority of which are started by lightning.

We've had wildfires in Canada for as long as I've been alive.  Some years they are bad; other years, they are manageable.  The worst year by number of fires was 1989; the worst year for total area burned was 2023.

Despite the human hazards and inconvenience, wildfires are essential to the health of our forests.  Some species (such as jack pine) require fire to reproduce.  Fire also contributes to biodiversity, and assists in disease and pest control.  While controlled burns are possible in some areas, they can present severe logistical challenges in remote areas, far from roads or other access points.

Perhaps instead of insulting and threatening Canadians, these politicians might send their condolences to Nicholas Dale's wife and children, who lost their husband and father just a few days ago fighting an out of control fire in Colorado. comments.name: Jerzy Szczypien
comments.body:
Nvidia, CUDA is much more than a programming language or software toolkit. It is a mature computing platform with millions of developers, decades of optimized libraries, and deep integration with virtually every major AI framework. Companies have invested enormous amounts of time and money building their software around CUDA. 

Rewriting, testing, and optimizing that software for a different platform is expensive, risky, and often provides little immediate benefit. That software ecosystem—not just NVIDIA's hardware—is why breaking NVIDIA's dominance is so difficult.

The statement, "Many of the new startups are developing chips tailored for inference," is technically true, but it misses the bigger picture. Designing an inference chip is only one piece of the puzzle. A successful AI hardware company also needs a complete software stack, developer tools, optimized libraries, customer adoption, and a sustainable business model. Without those, even excellent hardware may struggle to gain traction.

The Wall Street Journal article reads as if it were written for a fifth-grade audience: lots of cheerful optimism but very little substance. Saying that startups are "tailoring chips for customers" raises an obvious question: Which customers? Many of these companies have little or no meaningful revenue, a limited customer base, and negative cash flow. They may have promising technology and talented engineers, but commercial success requires far more than a compelling pitch.
